forest-city.story:
Forest City is a $100 billion housing project on the coast of Johor, Malaysia, about a 30-minute drive from Singapore. The Chinese developer Country Garden started it in 2016 and marketed it mainly to buyers in mainland China as a luxury home for 700,000 people.

It did not fill up. Country Garden told Bloomberg that 9,000 people lived there, while the magazine Domus reported in July 2024 that just over 1 percent of the development was thought to be inhabited. Business Insider reported that the company owed over $190 billion.

Malaysia then stepped in. On 20 September 2024 it launched a Special Financial Zone covering the area, with tax breaks from early 2025. They included a zero rate for family offices, private firms that manage the wealth of rich families, and lower personal income tax for some people who move there. Analysts quoted by BenarNews disagreed on whether this would work. The area also housed the Network School, a community of tech workers inspired by the idea of founding new countries online, until 22 July 2026. On that date a revocation by the Iskandar Puteri City Council took effect, ending its business licence and ordering it to stop operating, because the activities on the premises differed from those approved under its office licence. Johor's chief minister backed the decision and said no investor was above Malaysian law.

Forest City never sought sovereignty. It stays under Malaysian law with a state-backed tax arrangement, and it is included as a comparison. A huge private development remains an ordinary piece of a country, and the tax rules it depends on can be granted or changed by that country's government.

add_sources.t: Network School's licence revoked (The Star, 22 July 2026)

forest-city.why: Network School sentence had no listed source and little detail; added the date, the stated grounds and the source. Removed "briefly", which no source supports.

prospera-zede.story:
Próspera is a private business zone with its own rules on Roatán, a Caribbean island off the north coast of Honduras. It is the most fully developed recent attempt to get a country to hand over lawmaking to a private company, and its fate is being decided in court.

The legal path began in Honduras's own politics. An earlier plan, called Special Development Regions, was struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. In 2013 Honduras changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development (ZEDEs), areas with their own laws, courts and taxes.

Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Próspera with American venture capital, through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council. It offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land, and the project became a national issue.

Politics then turned. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, which means that they count as invalid from the start. That reach back in time is argued both ways. Brimen points to Article 96 of the Honduran constitution, which says a law has no retroactive effect except in some criminal cases, and to treaty promises he says protect the investments for at least 50 years. The constitutional lawyer Juan Carlos Barrientos answers that Article 96 concerns penalties such as prison and fines, and that the constitutional chamber may apply its rulings to the past.

Its owners had already claimed about $10.8 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. They relied on a legal stability agreement promising fixed rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024. Under President Nasry Asfura, who took office in January 2026, it rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026, and that return covers the country only from that date onward. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026, when the tribunal issued an order about a site visit, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute.

The case teaches what such a grant is worth. A country can give away lawmaking powers, and a later government and its courts can take them back. What the company holds is a right to seek money, under a treaty, if the taking breaks a promise. That is a large threat for a poor country, and critics and supporters disagree over whether it should exist. It does not amount to sovereignty for the zone.

add_sources.t: Zede en Honduras: inversiones en suspenso y disputa legal (El Heraldo, updated 29 October 2026)
Honduras ICSID Return: What It Means for Investors (Rio Times, 17 August 2026)

prospera-zede.why: Added who brought Honduras back to ICSID and that the return is not retroactive; replaced the flat "retroactive" statement with who argues what on retroactivity.

sark.story:
Sark is a small island in the Channel Islands, off the coast of Normandy, with about 500 people on 5.44 square kilometres, counting the neighbouring islet of Brecqhou. Cars are banned from its roads, and people use tractors, bicycles and horse-drawn carts. It is part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing Crown Dependency, a territory that belongs to the British Crown but is not part of the United Kingdom. It had a form of government that stayed feudal into the 21st century, and that is why it is here.

In 1565 Queen Elizabeth I granted it to Helier de Carteret, of Jersey, as a fief, land held from the Crown in return for service. His conditions were to clear out pirates and keep at least 40 loyal men there, so he rented out 40 plots called tenements. The arrangement stuck. The island's parliament, Chief Pleas, long consisted of the Seigneur, or feudal lord, the Seneschal, a judge, the 40 tenement holders and 12 elected deputies. So most seats went with land ownership. Its laws are based on Norman law.

The challenge came from outsiders who bought in. The billionaire brothers David and Frederick Barclay bought Brecqhou in 1993. In the mid-1990s they went to the European Court of Human Rights to challenge Sark's inheritance law, which required their island to pass to David's eldest son. Women gained equal inheritance rights in 1999. The brothers then argued that the whole system broke the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that protects basic rights in Europe. The feudal parliament was replaced under a new constitution in 2008. Sark stopped being a royal fiefdom. Candidates backed by the brothers' businesses won few seats in the elections of 2008 and 2010.

Sark is a useful counterexample for anyone drawn to old charters and private islands. Its self-rule was real and lasted over four centuries, yet the rules of the larger legal system still reached it. Owning a small island gave the Barclays private land and a court case, and it gave them no power to run the place.
sark.why: Sentence "It was replaced" had no clear subject.

hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.story:
Hawaii is a chain of Pacific islands that is now a state of the United States. For most of the 19th century it was an independent country. Kamehameha I conquered the islands between 1795 and 1810 and formed the Kingdom of Hawaii, and the United States and other powers formally recognised it. Disease and war cut the Native Hawaiian population by about 90 percent in the first century after contact with the West, down to 53,900 in 1876. American missionaries arrived in 1820 and gained great influence.

The sovereignty movement rests on what happened next. On 17 January 1893 a group made up mostly of Americans living in the kingdom overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, with the support of armed sailors landed from the warship USS Boston. An inquiry for President Grover Cleveland found that the American minister had helped the plotters and that most of the population opposed them, and a second report in 1894 cleared everyone except the queen. The plotters' government became the Republic of Hawaii in 1894. In 1898 the United States annexed the islands, and Native Hawaiians had no say in it. The movement regards both the overthrow and the annexation as illegal.

The modern movement grew in the 1960s and 1970s alongside other Indigenous campaigns. Its grievances included commercial development, corruption in the Hawaiian Homelands program, building on burial grounds and the bombing of Kahoʻolawe island.

It is a set of groups with different aims. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, started in 1987, runs like a government in waiting, with a constitution, elected offices, representatives for each island and Mililani Trask as its first governor. It reported 21,000 members in 1997 and led 10,000 people on a march to Iolani Palace in 1993, the 100th anniversary of the overthrow. The Nation of Hawaiʻi, led by Dennis "Bumpy" Kanahele, wants a republic where other groups prefer restoring the monarchy. It occupied the area around Makapuʻu lighthouse in 1989 and Kaupo Beach in 1993. It ended the second occupation in exchange for land in Waimānalo, where it built a village, a cultural centre and a puʻuhonua, a place of refuge. In 1995 the group sheltered an activist who refused to pay federal taxes, and Kanahele served eight months in federal prison and was barred for a time from the village. The state may negotiate over land, and federal criminal law still applies on it.

In 1993 Congress passed the Apology Resolution, which acknowledged that the overthrow was illegal. An apology is a statement and returned no land and no power. The United States Supreme Court addressed this in 2009. In Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs a unanimous court held that the resolution did not stop the state from selling the former crown lands of the monarchy. The next step offered was the Akaka Bill, first proposed in 2000, which would have begun federal recognition of a Native Hawaiian government, much like the relationship Native American tribes have with Washington. Under that model a people governs some of its own affairs while staying inside the United States. Many sovereignty groups opposed it because it would have treated past land transfers as valid, and Trask objected to its 20-year limit on claims against the United States. A 2005 Grassroot Institute poll found most Hawaii residents opposed it too.

In 2015 the Interior Department announced a procedure for recognising a Native Hawaiian government. A nonprofit, Naʻi Aupuni, planned an election of delegates to a constitutional convention, and opponents sued, arguing that an election limited to people of Hawaiian ancestry was race-based and unconstitutional. That November Justice Anthony Kennedy halted the counting of the votes. In December the organisers cancelled the election to avoid years of litigation and opened the convention to all the candidates. More than 150 of them attended a month-long gathering on Oahu in February 2016 and drafted a constitution. In March 2016 Naʻi Aupuni said it would not conduct a ratification vote and left the delegates to arrange one. Hawaii remains a state, and the groups remain divided between recognition within the United States and full independence. The case shows that winning an admission of wrongdoing from a government and winning back the power to rule are separate things, and a people seeking the second needs new law or a new negotiation.

add_sources.t: Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs (Wikipedia)
Na'i Aupuni cancels Native Hawaiian election (Hawaii Public Radio)
Na'i Aupuni bows out of ratification process (Hawaii Tribune-Herald, 17 March 2016)

hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.why: Story stopped at the 2015 stay. Added how the election and convention ended, and the 2009 Supreme Court ruling that answers what the Apology Resolution does in law.

mcgirt-v-oklahoma.story:
McGirt v. Oklahoma is a 2020 ruling by the United States Supreme Court about who may prosecute crimes across much of eastern Oklahoma. To follow it, a reader needs to know how American law treats tribal land. An Indian reservation is land Congress has set aside for a Native nation, and the law calls such land Indian country. Inside it, tribal and federal authorities handle many matters that a state would handle elsewhere. A federal law called the Major Crimes Act says that when a Native American commits one of the serious crimes it lists in Indian country, the federal courts try the case and the state courts do not.

Before Oklahoma became a state in 1907, about half its land, including today's Tulsa area, belonged to the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations, which had been forced there from the eastern United States along the Trail of Tears. Congress broke up much of their land into individual plots and passed a 1906 law that spoke of dissolving the tribal governments, while the same law kept them in force. For more than a century Oklahoma acted as though the reservations had ended.

The test case came from a prisoner. Jimcy McGirt, a member of the Seminole Nation, was convicted by an Oklahoma court in 1997 of sex crimes against a child in Broken Arrow and sentenced to life without parole plus 1,000 years. He argued that the crime took place on the Muscogee reservation, so the state had never had the power to try him. A similar case, brought by a Muscogee man named Patrick Murphy, had already reached the court, and Justice Neil Gorsuch had stepped aside from it because he had dealt with it as a lower court judge.

Gorsuch wrote the 5 to 4 decision. The rule he applied is simple. A reservation set up by Congress lasts until Congress clearly ends it. Allotting the land and pushing the tribe aside over the years do not count. The treaties promised the land, Congress had never said otherwise, and so the government was held to its word. Chief Justice John Roberts dissented. Oklahoma's Court of Criminal Appeals then applied the same reasoning to nine other Indigenous nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country.

The results reached the courthouse quickly. About 1,900 prisoners in Oklahoma fit the conditions of the ruling, though only around 10 percent qualified for a new hearing. Courts began throwing out old convictions and passing the cases to federal prosecutors. In August 2021, about 13 months after the Supreme Court's decision, the state appeals court ruled that McGirt did not apply to past convictions, which stopped that. An FBI agent working in Oklahoma said many cases handed over were going unprosecuted, and the state argued that tribal and federal offices lacked the staff. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that state courts share power with federal courts over crimes by non-Indians against Indian victims in Indian country, which took back part of what the state had lost. Disputes over the ruling's reach have continued. In May 2026 the Oklahoma Supreme Court rejected a settlement between the city of Tulsa and the Muscogee Nation over criminal jurisdiction on reservation land, because it lacked the approval of the governor and the state legislature.

The ruling did not set McGirt free. His state convictions were withdrawn and he stayed in custody for a federal trial in November 2020, where he was found guilty on three counts. In August 2021 he was sentenced to life without parole. In June 2023 the federal appeals court for the region, the Tenth Circuit, ordered a new trial because of the way testimony from the first trial had been introduced. He pleaded guilty in December 2023, his sentence was reduced to 30 years with credit for time served, and he was released in May 2024. He was arrested that August and pleaded no contest in Seminole Nation court to living somewhere other than his address on the sex offender registry, for which he received six months in the Seminole County jail.

For someone thinking about founding a territory, McGirt shows both the strength and the limit of old paper. A 19th-century promise can still bind a modern government if it was made by the right body and never properly withdrawn, and that took more than a century to establish. What it decided was which American court hears which case. The nations did not become independent states, and federal law still governs the land. A claimant with no treaty from Congress has nothing comparable to rely on.

add_sources.t: Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals rules that McGirt decision does not apply to past convictions (News On 6, 12 August 2021)
Oklahoma Justices Void Tulsa-Creek Jurisdiction Settlement (Law360, 29 May 2026)

mcgirt-v-oklahoma.why: "Less than a year later" was wrong (repeated from Wikipedia): the non-retroactivity ruling came in August 2021, about 13 months after McGirt. Added how McGirt's own case ended and the May 2026 Tulsa ruling.

nunavut.story:
Nunavut is Canada's largest territory, covering 2,093,190 square kilometres of the Arctic. Canada has provinces, which hold their own powers under the constitution, and territories, which get their powers from laws passed by the national parliament. Until 1999 this land was part of the Northwest Territories. It became its own territory because the Inuit, the Indigenous people of the region, negotiated for it.

In the 1970s Inuit organisations were pressing for recognition of their rights and for a settlement of their land claim, meaning their claim to land they had never formally given up. In 1976, during those talks, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and the federal government discussed splitting the Northwest Territories to give the Inuit a territory where they would be the majority. On 14 April 1982 a vote across the Northwest Territories backed division, and the federal government gave conditional agreement seven months later.

The land-claims agreement was finished in September 1992, and nearly 85 percent of voters in the area ratified it. In 1993 Parliament passed two laws, the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act. One settled the claim and the other set up the government. The official statute record says the Nunavut Act received royal assent, the formal last step in making a law, on 10 June 1993, while other accounts give 9 July 1993 as the date of passage. There was then a transition of nearly six years, and the territory began on 1 April 1999, with Iqaluit as its capital. The whole process took about 23 years from the first proposal.

In 2021 Nunavut had 36,858 people, of whom 84 percent were Inuit, and an estimated 43,091 in late 2026. Official languages are Inuktut, the Inuit language, along with English and French. Its assembly is elected without political parties and chooses a premier from among its members, and a council of elders advises on using Inuit knowledge in government. For its first 25 years the federal government kept control of public land and resources. A devolution agreement signed on 18 January 2024 hands that control to the territorial government.

Nunavut makes no claim to be a state. Its people remain Canadian citizens under Canadian law, and the territory exists because Parliament said so. The case shows what negotiation can achieve when a people has a recognised claim and a government willing to talk. It produced a government run by the local majority over an area larger than most countries, in exchange for staying inside the country, and it needed the consent of voters and of Parliament at every step.

add_sources.t: Nunavut Act, S.C. 1993, c. 28 (Justice Laws Website, Canada)

nunavut.why: Wikipedia's "passed 9 July 1993" conflicts with the statute record: the Nunavut Act received assent on 10 June 1993.

kasikili-sedudu-icj.story:
Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 square kilometres in the Chobe River on the border between Botswana and Namibia in southern Africa. No one lives there permanently, and floods cover it for several months a year from about March. It is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area.

The dispute came from a colonial document. In 1890 Germany and Britain signed the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty to settle their colonies in what are now Namibia and Botswana. The treaty said the line should follow the thalweg of the "main channel" of the Chobe. A thalweg is the deepest line of a river, the path boats follow. The river splits in two around the island, and the treaty did not say which branch was the main one. If it was the north branch the island lay in Botswana's half, and if it was the south branch the island lay in Namibia's.

When colonies became countries they inherited such lines, and the wording became their problem. On 17 May 1996 the two countries sent a joint letter to the International Court of Justice, the United Nations court for disputes between countries. Such a court can decide only if both sides agree to come, and they had signed a special agreement to do that. They asked it to decide the boundary under the 1890 treaty and the island's status.

Since the treaty gave no definition, the court worked one out from the river itself. It compared the two channels on depth, width, the volume of water they carried, the shape of the riverbed and whether boats could use them, looking at surveys from different periods. On 13 December 1999 it held, by 11 votes to 4, that the northern channel was the main one. The border therefore follows the deepest line north of the island, which places Sedudu in Botswana. The court added unanimously that citizens and boats of both countries are to receive equal treatment in the two channels around the island, so Namibians kept their use of the water.

The case shows how such quarrels really end. A river island is not empty land waiting for a claimant, because some treaty line already covers it. Even a vague colonial phrase binds the countries that inherited it, and the only open question is which of them holds the place. The two countries agreed in advance to put the question to a court, and only countries can bring a case there.

add_sources.t: Summary of the Judgment of 13 December 1999, International Court of Justice

kasikili-sedudu-icj.why: Added the judgment date, the vote and the unanimous second holding on equal treatment in both channels, from the court's own summary.

santa-rosa-island-amazon.story:
Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon River at the point where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, across the water from Leticia in Colombia and Tabatinga in Brazil. There are no bridges, because the river is wide and floods often and its banks keep moving, so almost everyone travels by boat. About 3,000 people live there. Peruvians from the surrounding province founded the settlement on 30 August 1974. It serves as Peru's border checkpoint for the area, and its economy rests on river trade, tourism and fishing.

Rivers make awkward borders because they move. Peru and Colombia drew their line in treaties from 1922 and 1929, and islands in the Amazon form and vanish over time. A treaty signed a century ago cannot name an island that did not exist yet, and that is the core of this dispute.

For decades Peru ran the place. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made the island a district of its Loreto region, with its own local government. On 5 August 2025 Colombian President Gustavo Petro wrote on social media that Peru had "appropriated it by law", and he warned that the change could cut Leticia, a town of nearly 60,000 people, off from the river. Petro's concern is that Leticia's use as an Amazon port depends on the channel beside it.

The two sides read the same treaties differently. Peru treats the island as an extension of Chinería Island, which the treaties did cover, so to Peru it is old Peruvian land. Colombia answers that Santa Rosa had not yet formed when the treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. It also argues that the border follows the deepest line of the Amazon and that new islands have formed on its side of that line. Colombia's foreign ministry says the two countries need to work together on deciding who holds each island.

In September 2025 the two countries' permanent border commission met in Lima and promised joint efforts to keep the Amazon navigable between Atacuari and Leticia, in a statement that did not mention the island directly. The island remains under Peruvian administration and disputed by Colombia. The case shows that new land in a border river does not become free for the taking. When a river produces an island, the neighbouring countries attach it to their own law, and a person hoping to claim it would find two governments already asserting it.

add_sources.t: Colombia y Perú se reúnen en Lima para garantizar la navegabilidad por el Amazonas (Noticias RCN, 13 September 2025)

santa-rosa-island-amazon.why: Added the later diplomatic step, the September 2025 border commission meeting.

aigues-mortes.story:
The Principality of Aigues-Mortes is a humorous mock state in the walled town of Aigues-Mortes in southern France, started on 21 June 2010 as a parody of Monaco to attract media attention and tourists.

Its founders invented a story based on the town's real history. King Louis IX of France obtained the town in 1240 by swapping property with the monks who owned it. He sailed from there on two crusades, in 1248 and 1270, and died of dysentery in Tunis on the second. According to the invented tale, on his deathbed he made his loyal squire, Pierrot Pitchoun, Prince of Aigues-Mortes. The current prince is styled Sovereign-Prince Jean-Pierre IV, said to be the 22nd in this line.

The practical side is ordinary. The group is registered in France as an organisation called LOUPAM. With local merchants and the town's tourist office, it runs an exchange, the Bourse princière, for a local currency, the flamant. It has attended micronation conferences in Perugia, Atlanta and Vincennes, and it hosted one in 2016.

No government recognises it, and the town remains part of France under French law. The case shows that a town can use the look of a state for promotion, and because it is open about the joke and works with local officials, nobody has a reason to object.

austenasia.story:
The Empire of Austenasia is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country, based in a suburban house in the London Borough of Sutton in England. Jonathan Austen, then a teenage student born in 1994, and his father Terry, a security guard turned gardener, founded it on 20 September 2008 by sending a declaration of independence for their house in Carshalton to their local Member of Parliament, Tom Brake. Terry became Emperor and Jonathan Prime Minister.

The first reply was silence. In May 2011 Jonathan met Brake, who asked Foreign Secretary William Hague what criteria Britain uses to recognise new states. Meanwhile Terry had stepped down in 2010, a successor had gone through a "civil war" and internal disputes, and a third leader held the post until January 2013, when Jonathan took the throne.

Jonathan began a program of growth, in which people around the world join by declaring their own home or a place they often visit part of the empire. It now claims dozens of properties, including houses in Britain, a holiday home in the Hebrides, part of a university campus in Australia, and places in the United States, Turkey and India. It claims to succeed the Roman Empire and has adopted Roman touches such as consuls and a senate, and Christianity was made its official religion in 2017. It sold commemorative coins for its tenth anniversary in 2018.

Jonathan stepped back in April 2024 and handed the running of it to a Prince Regent, Aggelos I. No government is known to recognise it, and the houses stay under the law of the countries they sit in. Each declaration is a private statement by the owner and moves no border.

holy-empire-of-reunion.story:
The Holy Empire of Reunion is an invented country created on 28 August 1997 by law students at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It claims Réunion, an island of about 2,511 square kilometres in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department of France, meaning a full administrative part of the French state.

The founders were on another continent, so nobody moved anywhere. The project has been described as a parody of the French department and as a simulation for practising politics and constitutional law. A Brazilian newspaper covered it in 1998 when it moved onto the internet.

It is not known to have tried to take control of the island or to have drawn any response from France, and whether the project is still active is not known. It is on the map as a claim on land already inhabited and governed, made from abroad as a study exercise.

kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.story:
Kiribati is a Pacific nation of low coral islands called atolls, with little soil. Nearly all its vegetables are imported. This is a purchase of farmland in Fiji by Kiribati's government, made with climate change in mind.

In May 2014 President Anote Tong said the government had made the final payment of 8.6 million American dollars for the Natoavatu Estate on Vanua Levu, one of Fiji's islands. The 2,210-hectare property, about 22 square kilometres, had belonged to the Anglican church and had once been a cattle and copra ranch worked by labourers from the Solomon Islands. It lies at the end of a dirt road about 55 km from the town of Savusavu, and about half of it is thick jungle. The money came from Kiribati's national savings fund of nearly A$1 billion. It was bought without review by Kiribati's parliament, for about four times the average price per acre of comparable land.

Tong described it as helping Kiribati's economic and food security as the climate changed. His environment minister said at the time that they were looking for a place that could hold 60,000 or 70,000 people. Scientists disputed the reasoning, saying sand atolls can rise with the sea.

Tong's successor, Taneti Maamau, took a different line. In February 2021 he announced that the land would return to being a commercial farm to feed Kiribati, with technical help from China. His government had switched its diplomatic ties from Taiwan to Beijing in 2019, so the news set off rumours that the land would pass to China. His office called those rumours a fabrication, and he ruled out any military use, saying China would only provide technical advice. Opponents asked him to be open about the plan, including who would farm it and for whom.

The law on this is plain. Buying land in another country gets a government the same thing it gets a private buyer, a title. Fiji remains the governing state, its law applies on the estate, and Kiribati holds it as an ordinary owner. So a nation that lost its land would still need the host country's agreement to move people there.

laas-en-bearn.story:
Laàs is a village of 135 people in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques area of southwest France, between Bayonne and Pau. It declared itself a principality on 1 January 2015. The mayor, Jacques Pédéhonta, first floated the idea in August 2011 in protest against government reforms of local government, and the village opposed the NOTRe law, a national reform meant to cut administrative costs. A list of micronations describes the move as a secession over neglect by the national government, while the mayor described it as a shared dream to support the local economy.

The mayor was open about how it worked. He told Sud Radio in 2018 that the village was not really a principality but acted as if it were. The legal basis is an ordinary association, registered as a non-profit with the prefecture in Pau in May 2014. The village adopted a constitution, a coat of arms and a motto, and placed a customs booth at its entrance, all without the consent of the French presidency, as he noted.

Visitors can buy a day in the principality. They cross customs, visit the château, walk a boulevard of stars in imitation of Hollywood and eat at the village inn. It received 28 buses in 2018, and a shop for local products and a passport were planned. Laàs is still a French commune with a French mayor, and the project shows a small place using a mock state as a tourism plan.

add_sources.t: Hayward, Under the Mermaid Flag: Achzivland and the performance of micronationality on ancestral Palestinian land, Coolabah, 2019

akhzivland.why: Philip Hayward is cited in the text but his article was not among the sources. Story unchanged. His abstract dates the declaration to 1972; the BBC and Ynet give 1971.

add_sources.t: Abbondanza, The Republic of Murrawarri and the Debate on Aboriginal Sovereignty in Australia, 2018

murrawarri-republic.why: The 2018 study cited in the text was not among the sources. Story unchanged. The repository page confirms the 2018 date, the author and the finding that the real claimed area is smaller than declared; it does not show the journal name, or the two area figures, on the page retrieved.

bunte-republik-neustadt.story:
The Bunte Republik Neustadt, German for Colourful Republic of Neustadt, was a mock state in the Äußere Neustadt district of Dresden, in eastern Germany. In June 1990 East Germany still existed, with both East and West German marks in use around reunification, and the mock state made fun of its symbols.

It was proclaimed for a neighbourhood festival on 22 to 24 June 1990. Gregor Kunz, who became its first monarch, said the idea came up in conversation at a pub on Alaunstraße and was put together within two or three months. A provisional government formed, led by a "monarch without portfolio" and ministers with joke titles such as minister for "unculture and submarines". It issued decrees and demanded annexation by the Vatican.

A white line painted on the streets marked its borders, around a block of the district, with signs announcing the free territory. It created a currency, the Neustadtmark, with exchange booths offering one Neustadtmark for one East German mark or two for one West German mark. Its flag showed a Mickey Mouse head in a wreath of wheat, modelled on the East German coat of arms.

In 1993 the government dissolved itself by "going bathing" in the River Elbe, a joke about its pollution. The state ended there, and the festival went on each June, much less political. The city's conditions and violence between left- and right-wing groups defeated several attempts to run it through an organising body, with national headlines in 2001 and 2002 and twelve police officers injured in 2007. Since 2002 it has had no single organiser, and each person or bar registers its own event with the city. It ran yearly until 2019, and none had been held since as of 2025. German law applied throughout, and the city licensed and policed the events like any others.
bunte-republik-neustadt.why: Added the later outcome: the festival has not been held since 2019.

glacier-republic.story:
The Glacier Republic is a mock state that the environmental group Greenpeace declared over Chile's glaciers on 5 March 2014, to push Chile into passing a law protecting them. Chile holds 82 percent of South America's glaciers. Greenpeace objected to mining companies building on or near them.

Its argument used the language of international law. Matías Asún, head of Greenpeace in Chile, said neither the constitution nor the water code names glaciers as a public good that must be protected, and Chile had no specific glacier law. So, the group said, there was a legal vacuum that let it found a country there, and it also pointed to unclear points in the border between Chile and Argentina. It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times. More than 40,000 people signed up as citizens within ten days, and it named embassies in about 40 countries, essentially the places where Greenpeace already had offices.

Greenpeace said the republic would hand the glaciers back to Chile once a suitable law passed. The legal gap may be narrower than claimed. The Civil Code makes all waters national public goods, and the Basic Environmental Law lists glaciers among protected areas, and Chile's government treats the glaciers as within its territory.

Six deputies introduced a glacier bill in 2014, and it was still being debated in late 2015. In 2018 the government withdrew it, with Environment Minister Marcela Cubillos saying glaciers should be protected through a general system of protected areas, and mining companies welcomed the move. Lawmakers took up a new bill in 2020, and that October a vote on it was delayed. Whether a law has since passed is not known. The republic works as advertising with a legal argument attached, and Greenpeace itself presents it as temporary.

add_sources.t: Glacier Law is withdrawn to push forward the creation of a protected area system (Fundación Glaciares Chilenos, 1 July 2018)
Chile's glacier protection bill faces new delays (Mining.com, 15 October 2020)

glacier-republic.why: Filled in part of the stated unknown: the 2014 bill was withdrawn in 2018 and a new one was taken up in 2020. The final outcome stays stated as unknown.

kalakuta-republic.story:
The Kalakuta Republic was the home compound of the Nigerian musician and activist Fela Kuti at 14 Agege Motor Road, in the Mushin area of Lagos, Nigeria. Nigeria was then ruled by the military. After returning from the United States in 1970, Kuti declared the compound independent of the state. The name mocked a prison cell called Calcutta in which he had been held, itself named after the Black Hole of Calcutta. The official Fela Kuti website differs on two points. It places this first compound in Surulere, another Lagos suburb, and says fellow prisoners gave a communal cell the name Kalakuta Republic in 1974, kalakuta being Swahili for rascal. The compound housed his family and band, a recording studio and a free health clinic.

Kuti's music attacked the government openly. His record Zombie compared soldiers to zombies who obey orders blindly, and it was popular in Nigeria and angered the head of state, General Olusegun Obasanjo. The military said it was unseemly to have a republic within a republic.

On 18 February 1977 about a thousand armed soldiers attacked, and the compound burned to the ground. Kuti's mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a second-floor window. She was taken to hospital, later fell into a coma and died of her injuries on 13 April 1978, about 14 months after the attack. The next year Kuti married 27 of his singers, who he said could not find work after the studio was burned and needed protection.

Kuti rebuilt Kalakuta in Ikeja, another part of Lagos, and lived there until his death in 1997. That three-storey house became the Kalakuta Republic Museum. His daughter Yeni and the architect Theo Lawson asked Governor Babatunde Fashola for help in 2011, he authorised a $250,000 grant, and the museum opened, still unfinished, on 15 October 2012, with his clothes, instruments and art, a rooftop café and guest rooms. His tomb is beside the house. No court ever considered the claim of independence. It was a political gesture against a military government, and that government answered with soldiers.

add_sources.t: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (Wikipedia)
The Kalakuta Museum (felakuti.com)

kalakuta-republic.why: Three errors. Her death read as about eight weeks after the raid, but she died on 13 April 1978, some 14 months later. The museum is not on the burned site: it is the later Ikeja house. The Fela Kuti website also gives a different location and name origin, now stated.

keraton-agung-sejagat.story:
Keraton Agung Sejagat, meaning Universal Grand Throne, was a mystical movement and invented kingdom based in Purworejo Regency, Central Java, Indonesia. Its founders, Totok Santoso Hadiningrat and Dyah Gitarja, began it in 2018 and gathered around 450 members.

Hadiningrat had tried a similar scheme before. In 2016 he founded the Jogjakarta Development Committee, promising members payments of 100 to 200 dollars a month from an account at a fictional Swiss bank. The money never came. This time he used history. He said a ruler of the old Majapahit Empire, a real kingdom in Java, had handed sovereignty, meaning supreme authority, to the Portuguese in 1518 on condition that it be returned after 500 years. Since those 500 years ended in 2018, he claimed authority over every country on Earth, with the United Nations as his legislature, the International Court of Justice as his judiciary and the Pentagon as his defence department. Members paid about 200 dollars each for uniforms and titles.

On 12 January 2020 the group held a public ritual in Pogung Juru Tengah township, and residents who were uneasy about it complained to the police. Officers came the next day, arrested the two founders on 14 January and named them suspects on the 15th. On 21 January Hadiningrat told a press conference that the kingdom was a scam and its history was made up. A University of Indonesia historian, Bondan Kanumoyoso, pointed out that the Majapahit Empire had collapsed in 1478, before the supposed treaty.

They were tried under a 1946 law against false news that causes public disorder and under the fraud article of the criminal code. On 15 September 2020 the district court in Purworejo found them guilty. Hadiningrat, named in court as Toto Santoso, received four years in prison, and Gitarja, named as Fanni Aminadia, received 18 months, both less than the five years and three and a half years prosecutors had asked for. They left custody in March 2021 when their period of detention ran out. The high court in Semarang and the Supreme Court upheld the verdict, and on 6 December 2021 they were arrested again in Sleman to serve the sentences. The group claimed the whole world, and neighbours' complaints to the police began the case that ended it.
keraton-agung-sejagat.mechanism: Selling titles on the strength of an invented treaty is treated as a matter for the police and the courts. Indonesian police acted on a local complaint, the founder admitted the scam, and the courts sent both founders to prison.

add_sources.t: Raja-Ratu Keraton Agung Sejagat Divonis 4 dan 1,5 Tahun Bui (CNN Indonesia, 16 September 2020)
Raja dan Ratu Keraton Agung Sejagat Kembali Ditangkap (CNN Indonesia, 6 December 2021)

keraton-agung-sejagat.why: Text said the outcome was unknown. Both founders were convicted in 2020, the verdicts were upheld, and they were re-arrested in 2021 to serve the sentences.

ladonia.story:
Ladonia is a declared country covering the area around large sculptures in the Kullaberg nature reserve in northwest Skåne, southern Sweden. In 1980 the Swedish artist Lars Vilks began building them there. Nimis, Latin for "too much", is made of 75 tonnes of driftwood. Arx, Latin for "fortress", is made of stone. The spot is so hard to reach that nobody found them for two years. The local council then ruled that they were buildings, which were forbidden on the reserve, and ordered them removed.

Vilks appealed repeatedly and lost, and the Swedish government finally settled the matter in the council's favour. Meanwhile the work changed hands. The artist Joseph Beuys bought Nimis in 1984, and after his death the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude bought it. Many local people, especially in tourism, supported the sculptures.

On 2 June 1996, in protest against the council, Vilks declared the area an independent country called Ladonia. In 1999 he built a third sculpture, Omphalos, of stone and concrete, a metre and a half high. A foundation complained to the police. In August 1999 a district court ordered Omphalos removed but refused to order the removal of Nimis and Arx, and the foundation appealed to the Supreme Court and lost.

The removal of Omphalos shows how Swedish law carried on working inside the claimed country. Vilks proposed blowing it up on Nobel Day in 2001 and applied for permission. Before the decision came out, he sold it to another artist, Ernst Billgren, who asked that it not be damaged. A crane boat hired by the state enforcement office took it away on 9 December, damaging it, and Vilks was billed 92,500 kronor.

Ladonia has a queen for life, an elected president and a language of two words, "waaaaalll" and "ÿp". It takes citizenship applications online and counted 22,858 citizens in 2020, from over 50 countries, none of whom live there. Vilks, who had police protection after threats over his drawings of Muhammad, died in a car crash in Markaryd, Sweden, on 3 October 2021, together with the two police officers guarding him. The declaration brought attention, and Swedish courts and agencies decided what stayed and what went.

add_sources.t: Lars Vilks (Wikipedia)

ladonia.why: Added the founder's death in 2021, missing from the text.

occupation-of-alcatraz.story:
Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay, California, best known for its federal prison, which closed on 21 March 1963. The next year the government declared it surplus property, meaning it no longer needed it. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie between the United States and the Lakota was read by them to mean that retired or abandoned federal land should go back to the Indigenous people who once held it. The island had also held Indian prisoners in the late 1800s and early 1900s, including 19 Hopi in 1895, which led one activist to say it was already Indian land in a way.

In 1963 Belva Cottier, a Rosebud Lakota social worker, read that the prison would close, and with her cousin Richard McKenzie she found a copy of the treaty. On 8 March 1964 a small group of Lakota occupied the island for four hours and proposed a cultural centre and an Indian university. A lawyer came with them to pursue a claim.

Five years later a loss brought the idea back. Plans for commercial development of the island were being discussed, and on 10 October 1969 the San Francisco Indian Center, which provided jobs, health care and legal help, burned down. Adam Fortunate Eagle planned a boat trip around the island for 9 November. Richard Oakes, an Akwesasne Mohawk, and LaNada Means, a Shoshone-Bannock student leader at Berkeley, joined with other students. Oakes and four others jumped from a yacht and swam, claiming the island by right of discovery, and the Coast Guard picked them up. That evening 14 people landed and stayed overnight. On 20 November about 100 people, 80 of them students from UCLA, began a full occupation under the name Indians of All Tribes.

They wanted the deed to the island, an Indian university, a cultural centre and a museum. They governed themselves as a community of people from many tribes, and John Trudell served as spokesman. Fresh water came by barge. Oakes left after his stepdaughter died in a fall on the island in January 1970, and as students went back to school, rival groups fought for control.

The federal government meanwhile hoped support would fade. In mid-1970, in secret talks, it offered part of Fort Miley in San Francisco, and the occupiers refused. It cut off the electricity and removed the barge that brought fresh water, and days later a fire destroyed several buildings. President Nixon approved a removal plan, and on 10 June 1971 federal marshals, FBI agents and police removed the last 15 people. No court ever accepted the treaty claim. Oakes was shot dead in 1972.

The island did not become Indian land, and the National Park Service now runs it. The Park Service says the occupation helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes, which sought to end tribes' legal status. The case shows a government ending an occupation by controlling water and power, and the same occupation helping to change national policy.
occupation-of-alcatraz.why: "It" in the Fort Miley sentence had no antecedent; named the federal government and that the talks were secret, per the National Park Service.

orania.story:
Orania is a town on the Orange River in the dry Karoo region of the Northern Cape of South Africa, 871 km from Cape Town, set up for Afrikaners, the Afrikaans-speaking white South Africans. Its background is apartheid, the system of legal racial separation in South Africa, which was in its last years in 1990.

The town began as a camp for workers on irrigation canals, built by the Department of Water Affairs in 1963. Most workers left after the project, and the town fell apart in the 1980s. Mixed-race and black families squatted there. In December 1990 about 40 Afrikaner families led by Carel Boshoff bought it for around R1.5 million. Boshoff, a right-wing academic, was a son-in-law of Hendrik Verwoerd, the prime minister known as the architect of apartheid, and founded the Afrikaner Volkswag in 1984. He believed that black majority rule could not be stopped. The 64 families living there, about 500 people, were evicted by the department before the buyers moved in. The first 13 settlers arrived in April 1991, to 90 houses in poor repair. Boshoff hoped that hundreds of thousands of Afrikaners would one day live there in a state of their own, called a Volkstaat.

The legal tool is private ownership, by a company set up for the purpose. To live there, a person must apply and be accepted as an Afrikaner, speak Afrikaans, have a clean criminal record and share the group's goals. All jobs, from management to manual labour, are done by Afrikaners, on a principle of self-reliance. Founders say this rejects the old system in which white people lived off black labour. CNN and other outside observers describe the town as whites-only and as an attempt to revive apartheid, a description the community disputes. Residents say they want to preserve their culture and protect themselves from crime.

In daily life the town grows pecan nuts, has pursued energy independence through solar power and has its own sewage works. It prints money-like coupons for use in its shops, and it has tried out a cryptocurrency. It keeps the last transitional representative council in the country, a form of local government left over from the end of apartheid. In 2016 CNN reported about 1,300 residents, and a local census in December 2025 counted 2,903, with growth estimated at 10 percent a year in 2019. The council has planned for 10,000.

The relationship with the state is unusual. On 23 April 1994 the Freedom Front and the two main parties signed an accord on Afrikaner self-determination. That led to section 235 of the South African Constitution, which guarantees a right of self-determination for cultural groups, and the MK Party gave notice in March 2026 that it intends to repeal it. In 1995 President Nelson Mandela visited for tea with Verwoerd's widow and said residents were entitled to run their affairs. A minister called the ideal of an Afrikaner cultural home within the Constitution legitimate in 1998. The South African government has said it opposes a whites-only community but has generally left the town alone. After Boshoff died in 2011, his son took over the Orania Movement.

Orania remains part of South Africa. It shows how far private land purchase can go toward a separate community, including control over who lives there, and it shows that this depends on a government choosing not to force the issue against its own equality principles.
orania.why: "Boshoff believed" appeared before Boshoff was introduced; moved the sentence after his introduction.
